title: feat: define how authority is withdrawn from a VAC
body:
> **Stacked on #29.** This branch is cut from `feat/vac-authority-credential`, because the section it changes exists only there. Until #29 merges, the diff against `main` shows #29's commits too; the change under review is the single commit `5833d4f`. Draft until #29 lands, at which point this rebases onto `main` and is ready.

## The gap

A VAC could not be taken back other than by waiting, and `validUntil` was only RECOMMENDED — so a VAC issued without one conferred authority that nothing could ever withdraw. The schema said as much in passing (*"authority that does not expire is authority nobody can withdraw by waiting"*) without requiring anything of an issuer.

The [[VDC]] section works the same problem carefully: `validUntil` REQUIRED, `credentialStatus` CONDITIONAL on a governing freshness window, revocation latency in Security Considerations, status lookups as a correlation surface in Privacy Considerations. The VAC section had none of it.

**The gap is worse for a VAC than for a VDC, which is why this is worth a PR rather than an editorial pass.** A VDC has a remedy the VAC does not: its verifier re-asks the permission question of the delegator at the time of the act, so withdrawing the delegator's own authority stops every delegate at once without touching a single credential. A VAC *is* that answer rather than a pointer to it. Nothing about the subject's current standing is consulted at verification, so expiry and revocation are the only remedies that exist.

## What this adds

**`validUntil` REQUIRED has moved to #29**, since a working draft should not publish a rule under which a conformant VAC confers authority nothing can withdraw. That leaves expiry as the sole withdrawal mechanism in #29, which is coherent standing alone, and this PR adds revocation on top of it. #29 carries an editor's note pointing here.

**`credentialStatus` is CONDITIONAL** on the freshness window the party governing the scope defines, mirroring the VDC rule.

**A new `### Withdrawal` subsection.** Expiry is the primary mechanism: it costs a verifier no network access, discloses nothing, and cannot fail open or closed, so it is the only withdrawal mechanism that survives the offline verification the VAC is built around. Only a VAC's issuer may revoke it — an attenuating holder revokes what it issued, the governing party revokes what it issued, neither reaches the other's directly.

**The verification rule is self-describing, which is the design decision here.** A verifier MUST check the status of every link that carries `credentialStatus` and MUST reject the chain if any is revoked; a link carrying none is evaluated on its validity period alone, and its absence is not a defect. The alternative — a status check per link — would have cost the VAC the property #29 spent the most text defending. Network cost now stays proportional to what a chain actually claims: one check for a long-lived root over short-lived attenuations, none where every link is short-lived. The two examples show exactly that contrast, the six-month root gaining a `credentialStatus` and the four-hour agent attenuation carrying none.

**Revocation cascades, and the section says so in both directions.** Revoking a VAC withdraws everything attenuated from it, transitively, whether or not the revoking issuer knows those derivations exist. That is what makes attenuation safe to permit without the governing party's involvement: it withdraws the whole tree in one act and needs no register of what its holder went on to issue. The converse is stated as plainly rather than buried — a chain whose links carry no status cannot show that an ancestor was revoked, so a verifier will accept an attenuation whose parent was revoked an hour ago. Offline verification bounds that exposure by the shortest `validUntil` in the chain; it does not remove it.

## Everywhere else the VDC's rules already reach

- **Attenuation** gains a SHOULD for short validity, since an attenuating holder is often a person, a device, or an agent rather than an operator of a status list, and may be unreachable when its grant needs taking back.
- **Relationship to the VDC** no longer claims the VAC chain is wholly offline. It is precommitted, with status on the links that carry it as the one live dependency. Overstating this was a small inaccuracy in #29 that this change would otherwise have made larger.
- **Security Considerations** gain items 19 and 20: revocation latency, and the cascade together with its invisibility where status is absent.
- **Privacy Considerations** gain item 14. Status on a root gives back part of what bearer-side presentation bought: whoever hosts the root's status list learns that a verifier checked it and when, so a governing party observes the *timing* of activity by agents and devices it never issued to and cannot see. One lookup for a whole chain rather than one per link, and timing rather than content — but it is the honest reason the section prefers short validity to status wherever re-issuance is available.
- **Governance Considerations** gain item 7, which is also the first VAC entry in that list: action vocabularies, the status mechanism, the freshness window, and whether status is required outright, are the governing party's to define.
- **Conformance Target 3** covers the status-checking rule alongside the chain rule.
- **CONTEXT.md** and the glossary entry follow.

## Not in scope, deliberately

**Resolved in #40, stacked on this branch.** The asymmetry below is settled there: the defaults should differ, and the control is an opt-out (`maxAttenuation`) rather than the VDC's opt-in `maxDepth`. Left here for the record.

**Attenuation is permitted by default; re-delegation is not.** A VDC prohibits re-delegation unless `maxDepth` explicitly authorises it (*"Setting `maxDepth` above 0 is the delegator's explicit authorisation to re-delegate; there is no other"*). A VAC permits attenuation unconditionally, capped at depth 8. That asymmetry may well be right — attenuation only ever narrows, and the cascade rule this PR states means a governing party can always withdraw the whole tree — but it is a deliberate difference that neither section argues for, and a governing party currently has no way to say "this authority is not attenuable". Worth settling separately; withdrawal is the control it leans on in the meantime, which is part of why this PR matters.

All `[[ref:]]` references, anchors, and JSON examples validated. Every commit carries a DCO sign-off.

title: spec(persona): a claim-type registry, and the two axes that key on it
body:
Attributes carry a type, a value and a provenance, and nothing saying how
carefully to handle either. So every consumer decides for itself whether a card
number renders in the clear — which is to say nobody decides.

## The gap that turned out to be underneath everything

Four separate things wanted somewhere stable to attach to — a mask format, a
sensitivity default, a release requirement, and any mapping to an external
vocabulary. All four key on the claim type, and `ClaimType` had a **pattern**
but no **registry**: nothing distinguished `phone.mobile` from `mobile.phone`,
and both validated.

So the registry comes first, not last. It's also the cheapest of the five
artefacts — a table and a document, no protocol change.

`claim-types.json` names 26 core tokens, each with expected `valueType`,
sensitivity, release requirement, mask style, minimum-set membership, and the
OIDC standard claims it answers. `CLAIM-TYPES.md` carries the reasoning.

It doesn't reopen the decision `ClaimType` already records — **the token stays
ours**, external vocabularies are mappings applied at presentation. It *records*
those mappings rather than adopting one, and keeps the two properties no flat
vocabulary has: a hierarchy (`payment.*` classifies a family without
enumerating it) and an open `x:` namespace, which exists because CardSpace's
fifteen fixed claim types is the specific way the prior art failed.

## Three axes, and they are not the same axis

| axis | question | where |
|---|---|---|
| **sensitivity** | how carefully shown **to the holder** | registry default, holder override |
| **release** | what it takes to let it **leave** | registry default, holder override |
| **linkability** | what it **costs** once gone | already computed — `correlation/analyze` |

A payment card is highly sensitive, release-gated, and barely linkable: every
card number is unique, so knowing one tells a second verifier nothing about the
first. A passport number is all three. Reading any one as a proxy for another
builds a consumer that hides the wrong things and warns about the wrong things.

## Store the override; derive the default

`sensitivity` and `release` are optional and their absence means *the holder did
not decide* — not `normal`. `attribute/put` MUST NOT persist a resolved default
in their place: an attribute recording one would keep it after the registry
tightened, so a reclassification would protect new attributes and leave existing
ones exposed.

An unregistered or `x:` token resolves conservatively. **That** is where
"absence is most restrictive" belongs — applied to a vocabulary nobody has
reasoned about, not to an unset field on a known type, where it would mask every
legal name and teach holders to hit reveal reflexively.

## The half that isn't cosmetic

`attribute/list` gains `includeSensitive`: a listing that asked for values still
omits the plaintext of a `high` attribute unless it asks for those too. Separate
from `includeValues` because the escalations answer different callers — a picker
wants every name and no card number, and shouldn't have to choose between
plaintext for everything and plaintext for nothing.

Masking a value you've already received defends a screen. It's no defence at all
against a log, a crash dump, or the memory of the process holding it.

## Release, enforced where it can be

`disclosure/present` MUST refuse a `stepUp` claim without a fresh approval bound
to **that `previewId`** — binding to the session would turn "each time" into
"once per login", which is the whole of what the requirement asks for. The new
`stepUpRequired` is retryable and does **not** consume the preview: refusing for
want of an approval must not cost the holder the decision they already made.

## Also: whoami reports capabilities

Effective, not stored — the question is "what may I do", and an entry that
narrows nothing means everything its role implies.

Without it, a client seeing only roles and scopes can't tell whether a caller
holds a capability its role doesn't imply, so it must either refuse a caller the
service would honour or offer everything and let the service refuse. Not
hypothetical: the console did the former until vta-browser-plugin#183.

## The rule the new persona conventions state

> **A response may name identity; it may not carry identity.**

A persona's label, a face's name, an attribute's type — names. Values are
content, returned by exactly three tasks. whoami is worth naming because it's
the one a maintainer is most tempted to extend: a convenience display-name
member would make an authority endpoint an identity endpoint, and every consumer
already logging its response would begin logging identity.

## Scope note

Existing stored attributes are expected to be lost — we're the only implementer
and still in active development — so the 1.0 schemas are amended in place rather
than versioned. Shout if you'd rather I minted `/2.0`.

## Open questions in the doc rather than decided here

- Should `release: "never"` exist — held for reference, never disclosable? It's
  useful and honest, but makes the pool partly a password manager, and that's
  easier to add later than remove.
- Should the agent *serve* the registry (`persona/claim-types/list`, the shape
  `renderers/list` already has)? Clients can ship it statically today; worth
  doing when the first extension type ships.

## Checks

`npm run validate` — 403 specs, 68 shared schemas, clean. Rust and TS bindings
regenerated (`cargo run -p trust-tasks-codegen`, `npm run build-ts-bindings`)
and committed; `cargo test -p trust-tasks-rs` 14 suites green.

title: fix(console): re-sync the claim table with the registry it reported
body:
fix(console): re-sync the claim table with the registry it reported

This console vendored the claim-type registry while it was still a draft, and
reported three holes in it rather than patching around them locally. The
registry gained the fixes (trust-tasks#377); this takes them.

**The prefix walk exists now.** `treatmentOf` had a long comment explaining that
there was no prefix fallback and that inventing one locally would make this
console less careful than the registry asked. That reasoning was right and is
now stale: rule 3 walks the longest registered prefix and takes the *more
protective* of it and the unregistered floor, per axis.

The direction is the whole of what makes it safe, and both halves are pinned:
`payment.giftCard` inherits the family, because a gated family must not be
leavable by inventing a token; `name.somethingNew` does **not** inherit `name`'s
`none` and stays masked, because a family entry that could loosen would turn a
friendly prefix into a way to unmask. An exact entry still wins outright, or
every registered member of a strict family would flatten to the family's own
treatment and the table would say nothing.

**Masking no longer requires `high`.** The two were one axis, which left
`email.*` carrying an `emailLocal` style no rule could ever apply while the
registry used `a•••@example.com` to motivate itself. They are two strengths:
`high` means withheld from a listing that did not ask, a mask style means not
shown in the clear. An email address is worth hiding from the person behind you
without being worth withholding from every listing.

**A bare `name` is a token.** A pool keeping one undifferentiated name was
masked in full.

Seven tests, because none of this was covered — the existing ones pin the mask
*formatter* and the transcription, and every one of them passed both before and
after the behaviour changed. Also `x:payment.card` now has a test: the extension
namespace must not be able to borrow a family any more than it can borrow an
entry, or a core token spelled with a prefix would pick up a *looser* mask than
the floor.

title: feat(setup): ask for the grant the identity pane needs
body:
Splits the functional half out of #278, so it isn't waiting on a vocabulary
decision. **No naming changes here** — this is the reason most of the pane
shipped in #277 cannot work.

## The problem

Setup provisions a **context-scoped** admin — `pnm contexts create --admin-did`
writes `allowed_contexts: ["openvtc"]` — while the attribute pool, the profiles
over it and the disclosure history are gated on an **unscoped** holder
credential, because they sit above every trust context.

So Attributes, Profiles and Disclosures are refused on every install today.
Correctly: the gate is the boundary working. But the only way to satisfy it was
to make OpenVTC an administrator of *every* context on the agent — a real
escalation for a community client, and not something to document as the happy
path.

## The fix

Upstream, **verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1286** adds
`Capability::PersonaHolder`: granted by name, conferred only by a super admin,
and additive — it grants authority over the holder's own identity *without*
granting authority over other contexts.

Here:

- the setup screen's command ends `--admin-holder`;
- for installs that already exist, the pane's refusal carries the command rather
  than only the agent's (accurate, abstract) explanation. It matches the phrase
  both the current and the pre-capability VTA use, so either agent produces the
  hint — and matches that phrase rather than "forbidden", because a false
  positive sends someone to fix something that is not their problem;
- the command is now **tested**. It is pasted character for character into
  another terminal, and a mangled string literal — a run of spaces where a line
  continuation collapsed — is invisible in review and survives to the operator's
  shell. One had already got in while writing this.

## Merge order

Harmless before #1286: `--admin-holder` is refused by an older VTA with a clear
error, and the pane behaves exactly as it does today. Useful after it.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide §9)

```
- [x] No new clients/timeouts (R1.2) — no new network calls
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Retries bounded (R1.4) — none added
- [x] Loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — n/a
- [x] Acks after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] Wire types (R3.*) — none changed
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*) — unchanged; the hint is display
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*) — the hint is shown only
      for the refusal it actually addresses
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" (R2.1) — n/a, no new mutation
- [x] Deviations — none
```

`cargo test --workspace` green (425 in the binary), clippy clean.

body:
spec(persona): a claim-type registry, and the two axes that key on it (#377)

* feat(persona): a claim-type registry, and the two axes that key on it

A holder's attributes carry a type, a value and a provenance, and nothing that
says how carefully to handle either. Every consumer therefore decides for
itself whether a card number is shown in the clear — which is to say, nobody
decides.

Four mechanisms wanted somewhere stable to attach to: a mask format, a
sensitivity default, a release requirement, and any mapping to an external
vocabulary. All four key on the claim type, and the claim type had a *pattern*
but no *registry* — nothing distinguished `phone.mobile` from `mobile.phone`,
and both validated.

## The registry

`claim-types.json` names 26 core tokens with, for each, the expected
`valueType`, a sensitivity, a release requirement, a mask style, whether it is
in the minimum set, and the OIDC standard claims it answers.
`CLAIM-TYPES.md` carries the reasoning.

It does not change the decision `ClaimType` already records — the token stays
ours, and external vocabularies are mappings applied at presentation. It
*records* those mappings rather than adopting one, and keeps the two properties
no flat vocabulary has: a hierarchy (so `payment.*` classifies a family without
enumerating it) and an open `x:` namespace.

## Three axes, kept apart

- **sensitivity** — how carefully a value is shown *to its own holder*
- **release** — what it takes to let it *leave*
- **linkability** — what it *costs* once gone (already computed, by
  `correlation/analyze`)

A payment card is highly sensitive, release-gated and barely linkable — every
card number is unique, so knowing one tells a second verifier nothing about the
first. A passport number is all three. Reading any one as a proxy for another
builds a consumer that hides the wrong things and warns about the wrong things.

## Store the override; derive the default

`Attribute.sensitivity` and `Attribute.release` are optional, and their absence
means *the holder did not decide* — not `normal`. A consumer resolves absence
from the registry, and `attribute/put` MUST NOT persist a resolved default in
its place: an attribute that recorded one would keep it after the registry
tightened, so a reclassification would protect new attributes and leave the
existing ones exposed.

An unregistered or `x:` token resolves to the conservative answer. That is where
"absence is most restrictive" belongs — applied to a vocabulary nobody has
reasoned about, not to an unset field on a known type, where it would mask every
legal name and teach holders to reveal reflexively.

## The half that is not cosmetic

`attribute/list` gains `includeSensitive`. A listing that asked for values still
omits the plaintext of a `high` attribute unless it also asks for those.
Separate from `includeValues` because the two escalations answer different
callers: a picker wants every name and no card number.

Masking a value already received defends a screen. It is no defence at all
against a log, a crash dump, or the memory of the process holding it — the
control that matters is the one deciding whether the plaintext is sent.

## Release, enforced where it can be

`disclosure/present` MUST refuse a `stepUp` claim without a fresh approval bound
to **that `previewId`** — `stepUpRequired`, retryable, and the preview is not
consumed, since refusing for want of an approval must not cost the holder the
decision they already made. Binding to the session instead would turn "each
time" into "once per login", which is the whole of what the requirement asks
for.

## Also: whoami reports capabilities

Effective, not stored — the question is "what may I do", and an entry that
narrows nothing means everything its role implies.

Without it a client seeing only roles and scopes cannot tell whether a caller
holds a capability its role does not imply, so it must either refuse a caller
the service would honour or offer every action and let the service refuse.
Both are live problems: the console does the former today.

The persona conventions state the rule this sits under — **a response may name
identity; it may not carry identity.** whoami answers what a producer may do,
never who they are made of.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.gore@gmail.com>

* spec(persona): close three holes the first consumer of the registry found

The console's masking work was the first thing to read this table rather than
write it, and it found three defects in a single sitting. All three are the
same shape: prose that claimed a property the data did not have.

**A gated family was leavable by inventing a token.** §2 said the hierarchy
makes `payment.*` classify as one family "without enumerating its members" and
a future token "safe by construction", and §4 never consulted a prefix. So
`payment.somethingNew` fell to the unregistered default — whose `release` is
`consent`, weaker than every registered member of the family it plainly belongs
to. Sensitivity degraded safely; release degraded the wrong way, silently.

Resolution now walks the longest registered prefix, and takes the **more
protective** of it and the floor, per axis. "More protective" rather than "the
prefix wins" so a family entry can only ever tighten: `name` as a prefix does
not make an unregistered `name.somethingNew` visible. `payment` and `gov` gain
family entries.

**A mask style no rule could apply.** `email.*` carried `emailLocal` while §3.1
defined masking as something `sensitivity: high` means — and §1 used
`a•••@example.com` to motivate the whole registry. Masking and withholding were
tangled into one axis; they are two strengths of protection, not one. Masking is
now independent of sensitivity, so an email address can be hidden from the
person behind you without being withheld from every listing.

**No entry for a bare `name`.** A pool keeping one undifferentiated name got it
masked in full — correct under the old rule 3, and a sharp edge for the first
real pool. `name` is now an exact token as well as a family prefix.

Also: `defaults` had two identical keys (`unregistered`, `extension`) with
nothing saying which an `x:` token used, and nothing said whether a mask applies
to a stored value or a rendering. One key now, and it applies to a rendering.

title: feat(console): hide sensitive fact values behind a per-fact Show
body:
feat(console): hide sensitive fact values behind a per-fact Show

The persona pane draws the holder's own facts, so a passport number, a
mobile number and a date of birth sit on screen for as long as the pane is
open — through a screen share, a screenshot pasted into an issue, and
anyone walking past the desk. Which of those is sensitive is a property of
the claim type, and the claim-type registry now says so.

`manager/claim-sensitivity.ts` carries a vendored copy of that registry's
masking data — sensitivity and mask style per token, from
specs/persona/_shared/0.1/claim-types.json at registryVersion 0.1. Vendored
because the agent does not serve the table: `persona/claim-types/list` is
an open question in CLAIM-TYPES.md §6, deferred until the first extension
type ships, and clients ship it statically until then. Only the two members
this console reads are transcribed, so a re-sync is a diff against that
file rather than a rewrite.

An unregistered or `x:` token resolves to the conservative default,
`high`/`full`, per §4 rule 3 — and there is deliberately no prefix walk.
claim-types.json declares only leaves and §4 consults no prefix, so
inventing a `payment.*` family rule locally would make an unknown member of
that family show *more* than the registry asks, not less.

Every value the pane draws now goes through one `FactValue`, and
`formatValue` is no longer exported, which makes that structural: a card
that hides a number while the strip below prints it in full has hidden
nothing, and the second surface is always the one added later. Reveal is
per value, in that component's own state — never a global unmask, and
nothing that outlives the element, so navigating away re-hides everything.
A hidden value is drawn at full strength with a mask glyph; `c.faint` stays
the pane's word for "the agent sent no value", because a fact the holder
has must not look like one they do not.

**This is not a security control.** The value was fetched into the page
before any of it ran; masking changes what is drawn, never what the page
holds. It defends against a shoulder, a screenshot and a screen share, and
that is the whole scope. The control that would matter is a read-path one —
`includeSensitive` on `persona/attribute/list`, so a listing that did not
ask is answered without the values — and it does not exist yet. The module
doc says so at length so that nobody reviewing this later mistakes the
visible half of a control for the control.

The render fixture moves from a bare `name` to `name.legal`: the registry
has no entry for the former, so it now resolves to the conservative default
and those assertions would have been reading a mask.

title: feat(rooms)!: let a community decide whose rooms it hosts
body:
The first of the data-room gaps the guide had to warn about. #1274 made a registration prove who its owner is — which stops anyone registering a room in *somebody else's* name, but nothing stopped a stranger registering one in their own, on a community that had never met them. §7.4 says a VTC governs what its members may create on it; this is that, in the policy engine the service already has.

### A new policy purpose, not a new mechanism

`rooms` joins the ten existing purposes — bundled default, active-policy row, `POST /v1/policies` to replace it. `handle_create` assembles facts, loads the active policy, and refuses on a deny **with the policy's own code**, so a refusal names the rule that produced it.

The shipped default hosts `open` and `attributed` for the community's own members and refuses `private` until an operator activates a policy permitting it. Not because a private room is dangerous, but because a community that has not decided should not discover it is hosting rooms whose membership it cannot see.

### Why this does not break invariant I5

I5 — room authorization never touches a host's ACL — is what makes a room portable, and it holds. Creation is the exception the design names, and it is a different question: a host refusing to store a room is not deciding who belongs to it (the room does not exist yet and has issued nothing), it is deciding whether to lend its disk.

`govern_creation` is the only place in the rooms handlers that reads the roster, it runs **before** the room exists, and no operation on an existing room consults it. A standalone `room-host` has no policy engine and no roster at all — T1's governance is its owner, which is the whole model.

### Three refusals, all closed rather than open

| | |
|---|---|
| A policy that answers **nothing** | Deny. Rego is permissive about a missing rule; reading an empty result as "no objection" would turn a typo in a package name into an open host |
| A **threaded** verdict (`refer` / `request-more`) | Deny. Registration is one synchronous call with no thread to resume, so a verdict this surface cannot carry out is refused rather than approximated |
| **No active `rooms` policy** | Deny — *not* a 500. `install_defaults` fills the row at boot, so the gap means a first boot that has not reached it or a deleted row; both are a closed door, and the message says which, so an operator checks their policy list rather than their credentials |

### What a policy can see

The creator (DID, whether a member row exists, their ACL role) and the room's identifier, visibility and owner. **Not** the design's `didControlledBy` / `contentStoredAt` hosting axes: the published `rooms/create/0.1` schema has no member for either, so no host can know them, and inventing them locally would put this service's rooms out of conformance with the schema every other host reads. Worth a look in review — if those axes matter, they need to go upstream first.

### Tests

Seven unit tests on the decision (each default-policy branch, the no-decision refusal, the threaded-verdict refusal, the verification gate) and two at the wire: a stranger's perfectly-valid registration is refused **and leaves no room row**; a member is refused `private` until the community enables it, after which the same request succeeds.

Existing room tests now seed a member row for the fixture owner — they were creating rooms as strangers, which is exactly what this refuses — and the private-tier tests activate a permissive policy, which doubles as the worked example of enabling the tier.

`cargo test -p vtc-service --no-fail-fast`: 952 lib + every integration suite green; the only failures are the four known `VTC_SKIP_ADMIN_UI_BUILD=1` artefacts. `clippy --all-targets` and `fmt --check` clean.

### Breaking

`PolicyPurpose` gains a variant (its `ALL` array goes 10 → 11), so an exhaustive downstream `match` needs an arm. A VTC that upgrades installs the new default at boot; one that somehow has no `rooms` row refuses room creation until it does, rather than serving it ungoverned.

title: refactor(persona): the copy outside the pane speaks the vocabulary too
body:
Third of three PRs bringing the persona vocabulary into sync across the stack:

- verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1291 — `pnm persona …`
- vta-browser-plugin#183 — the console's persona pane (which was also *stale*)
- **this one** — the OpenVTC copy outside the identity pane

#280 brought the pane over and left the rest for "when next touched".

## What changed

The join flow's identity choice — *"Who should this community know you as?"*,
*"Choose the persona this community will know you as"*, *"Already known to:"*,
*"Be someone new to this community"* — the invitation list, and the communities
panel's empty state.

**The reuse warning is the one that matters.** It is the last thing a person
reads before linking themselves across two communities, and it now carries the
table's sentence verbatim:

> Being known here as "Work me" makes you the same person to anyone who sees
> both this community and the others using it.

The point of a fixed phrase is that meeting it twice teaches it. A paraphrase in
one surface spends the recognition and gives nothing back.

## What I deliberately left alone

**`profile` in setup, backup and `--profile`.** That is the *config profile* — a

title: test(console): render the panes
body:
Eleven persona PRs today, and **every bug that reached the live console lived in the one layer nothing could test**:

| what shipped | what saw it |
|---|---|
| a `ref` callback that looped the renderer to a blank page (#179) | you, within a minute |
| a form that opened empty because a selection was never passed to it (#182) | you |
| a screen that never came back because its mode was decided once (#178) | reading, just in time |
| a field asking for an identifier the context did not have (#181) | you |

The models under all of them — `identity-graph`, `profile-entries`, `persona-flow`, `persona-candidates` — passed throughout, because each was correct. Rendering is the only thing that sees the rest.

## What this adds

`tests/harness/` — module hooks and a DOM so `node --test` can mount a pane. Nothing changes about how tests elsewhere are run or written.

**The hooks** do two things that are not obvious:

- resolve a `./thing.js` import to `thing.tsx`. The sources use TypeScript's `Bundler` resolution, which the bundler honours and Node does not; existing tests sidestepped it by importing `../src/.../thing.ts` with the real extension, which a component cannot do because its *own* imports are written the other way.
- transform JSX with **esbuild**, not `typescript`. This repo is on TypeScript 7, whose JS API is the native port's small surface — `transpileModule` and `JsxEmit` are simply not on it, and a hook written against the 5.x compiler API fails with an undefined enum that names nothing.

**The fake agent** answers by task URI, returns the relay's real envelope (`{ok, result: {kind: "accepted", …}}`) so a pane that mishandles a real response cannot pass, and **throws** on a task the test did not name — a pane asking something unexpected is exactly what a test should notice, so that is a failure rather than an empty answer.

## The tests

Nine, each written against **the symptom a person saw** rather than the fix, so they keep meaning something if the fix is rewritten. Every negative is paired: *"a context with no identifier offers to create one"* sits beside *"a context with identifiers lists them"*, because the first alone passes against a form that always offers to create.

**Mutation-checked against three of the real bugs:**

- restoring the scrape-from-a-`ref` → **3 tests fail** (the loop takes the whole pane down, which is what it did)
- dropping the create offer → *a context that publishes no identifier offers to make one* fails
- ignoring the selection → *selecting a persona aims the context's button at it* fails

## Two harness details that quietly made a test lie

Both cost me a false pass before they were fixed, and both are written down:

- **Click a checkbox; do not assign `checked`.** React reads the click. A hand-set value plus a synthetic `change` looks like a tick to the test and like nothing to the component — the test passed while proving nothing about the handler.
- **Text matching takes the innermost element.** Document order returns an ancestor, so clicking a card where the test meant a row inside it selects the wrong thing and then asserts against the wrong screen.

## Cost

One devDependency (`happy-dom`), scoped to the extension package. The extension's `test` script gains `tsc -b`, matching `packages/core`'s, because the render tests import through the real package and need its `dist`.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npm run build`, `npm test` — **865 across four workspaces** (extension 260 → 269). All six `ci.yml` assertions against the real build.

title: refactor(pnm): persona commands read in the words a person uses
body:
Part of a sweep bringing the persona vocabulary into sync across VTI, the
browser plugin and OpenVTC. `design-docs/persona-vocabulary.md` names
`pnm persona …` as known drift "until next touched" — this touches it.

## Where I drew the line, and why

**Commands and flags keep the spec's words.** `persona profile put
--profile-id` names `persona/profile/put/1.0`. A command that did not would be a
second name for a task, drifting from the URI it sends and from every script
already written against it.

**What an operator reads uses the person's words.** attribute → *fact*,
profile → *face*, binding → *wearing*.

So `persona profile list` prints `Faces:` above JSON whose members are
`profileId`. That pairing is deliberate rather than an oversight: it is the one
place both halves are on screen together, and therefore where an operator learns
the mapping. The module header records the reasoning so the next person doesn't
"fix" it back.

If you'd rather draw that line elsewhere — labels matching the command instead —
say so; it's a one-line change per label and I'd rather agree the rule than
argue it per string.

## What changed

- printed labels: `Attributes:` → `Your facts:`, `Profile:` → `Face:`,
  `Disclosures:` → `What has left:`, `Correlation:` → `Links:`
- the hints beside them, including the two destructive paths, which now carry
  the table's sentence: *"Nothing already shared is affected — that has left."*
- the disclosure preview's prose — the most-read screen here: *"Before anything
  leaves — nothing has been sent."*, `Linkable` → `Linked`
- `--help` for every persona subcommand
- the reused phrases the table asks for verbatim: *"a context only ever gets a
  copy"*, *"same person to anyone who sees both"*

## One thing that was simply wrong

The top-level help said the holder-scoped tasks need *unrestricted* authority.
That stopped being the only way when `persona-holder` landed (#1286) — it now
names both.

## Pre-merge checklist (vti-stack-development-guide §9)

```
- [x] No new clients/timeouts (R1.2) — text only, no call sites changed
- [x] No lock held across a network await (R1.3)
- [x] No local state before its remote effect (R2.1)
- [x] Retries bounded (R1.4) — none added
- [x] Loops survive transient errors (R1.5) — n/a
- [x] Acks after durable handoff (R1.6) — n/a
- [x] Wire types (R3.*) — unchanged; command and flag names deliberately kept
- [x] Config absence = most restrictive (R5.*) — unchanged
- [x] Logs/status claim only what was verified (R6.*) — the preview's
      "nothing has been sent" and the unbind warning keep their exact meaning
- [x] "Process dies on the next line" (R2.1) — n/a
- [x] Deviations — none
```

title: feat(secrets)!: cache seed reads so KMS traffic scales with time, not requests (#1290)
body:
feat(secrets)!: cache seed reads so KMS traffic scales with time, not requests (#1290)

The BIP-32 master seed is read on every key-touching request. `load_seed_bytes`
has ~25 call sites — the signing oracle, key mint/rotate/list, the holder-key
paths, every did:webvh lifecycle operation — and each one calls `SeedStore::get`
with no memoization.

On the local backends that is free. On AWS Secrets Manager every read is a
`GetSecretValue`, and every `GetSecretValue` is one billed KMS `Decrypt` against
the key protecting the secret. So KMS request volume tracked request volume: a
VTA sustaining ~22 req/s bills ~58M KMS requests a month re-reading a value that
never changed. That is what prompted this — an observed 58.1M-request line item.

`[secrets] cache_ttl_secs` (default 60, `0` disables) bounds how long a
successfully-read seed is reused from memory. Same VTA, ~43k backend reads a
month instead of 58M.

What makes reuse safe. The seed for a generation is immutable — it changes only
on rotation — so the cache skips a re-read of a constant rather than gambling on
a moving value. On top of that:

- Writes invalidate. This is load-bearing, not hygiene: `operations::seeds::
  rotate_seed` writes the new seed and then *immediately* re-reads it to
  re-encrypt every imported secret. A cache surviving the write would
  re-encrypt them under the wrong key.
- A read that raced a write is discarded via a generation counter, so it can
  never install a superseded seed for a full TTL. Signing runs concurrently
  with rotation, so this case is real.
- `Ok(None)` and every error pass straight through. Caching "absent" would make
  a transient backend outage indistinguishable from an unprovisioned VTA for the
  whole TTL and would race first-boot provisioning.
- The cached copy is zeroized on eviction and drop (P0.7); the TTL doubles as
  the bound on how long the seed sits resident.

The trade-off, documented rather than glossed: the seed is now resident for up
to the TTL where it was previously resident per-operation. On a busy VTA that is
a distinction without a difference; on a quiet one it is a real if small
widening. `cache_ttl_secs = 0` restores the old behaviour.

Also fixes the same defect class one layer down (R1.2): the AWS, GCP, Azure and
Kubernetes backends each built a client — and re-resolved credentials — on every
call, an IMDS/STS or kubeconfig round trip on top of the API call. Each now
builds once via `OnceCell`, which is what the Vault backend already did.

The TEE path is unaffected: `KmsTeeSeedStore` is constructed directly by
vta-enclave and already holds the seed in enclave memory, so it is not wrapped.
The VTC needs no equivalent — it reads its key bundle once at boot.

BREAKING CHANGE: `SecretsConfig` is now `#[non_exhaustive]`, so struct-literal
and functional-update construction are no longer available outside vti-secrets.
Build from `SecretsConfig::default()` and assign. Taken deliberately while a
break was already being made: this struct has grown a field per backend and
will keep growing, and marking it now makes every future field additive.

title: fix(persona): the audit trail says what changed, and correlation/analyze conforms
body:
Two fixes to the `persona/*` trust-task slice. They are separate commits and read independently, but they share a shape: in both cases the slice was producing an answer that was technically a response and practically not usable.

## 1. The audit trail says what changed

A user looked at the console's audit pane and could not tell what a persona operation had done. `audit_persona` called `audit::record(...)` — which has no `detail` parameter — so every persona row was an action name, an actor, an opaque ULID and `success`. Twenty rows of `persona.attribute.put` against twenty identifiers, with no way to distinguish a create from an update, a cascade delete from a no-op against a typo'd id, or a `binding/set` that materialised forty claims from one that cleared them.

The console side was never the defect. `impl From<&AuditLogEntry> for AuditEnvelope` already surfaces `detail` as `detail.reason` and the audit pane renders it in full. There was nothing to render.

The write handlers now go through `audit::record_with_detail` and say what changed:

| task | detail |
|---|---|
| `attribute/put` | created-or-updated, claim type, valueType, provenance kind, resulting version |
| `attribute/delete` | whether it existed, cascade or not, how many profiles it was removed from |
| `profile/put` | created-or-updated, entry count, resulting version |
| `profile/delete` | whether it existed, whether unbind was asked for, how many personas were unbound |
| `binding/set` | the profile bound or "unbound", materialised claim count, version |
| `local/profile/put` | created-or-updated, entry count, version, whether it matches a pool value |
| `local/profile/delete` | whether it existed, how many personas were unbound |
| `local/binding/set` | the local profile bound or "unbound", version |

Reads still pass `None`. A read changes nothing, and a sentence restating the request is noise in an append-only store.

### Why the value stays out — and why the usual reason is the wrong one

The rule that the attribute VALUE is never recorded is not new. What is new is that `audit_persona` now explains it, at length, because the reason people reach for first is false here and does not survive contact with an operator asking for a better trail.

The reason is **not** access control. Persona rows are recorded with `context_id: None`, and `operations::audit::authorize` already refuses any entry not confined to a named context to anyone but an unrestricted (super) admin — precisely the caller `Reach::Holder` admits to `attribute/list`, which hands back the plaintext values on request. Nobody gains a read by us writing one into the log.

The reason is **lifetime**. The audit keyspace is append-only and pruned on its own retention schedule (`vta_audit::cleanup_expired_logs`); the pool is deleted when the holder deletes an attribute. Copy a value across and `attribute/delete` quietly stops being a delete — the value outlives the record it came from, in a store the holder's delete does not reach and which is not rewritten afterwards.

Stating that distinction is the point of the comment. "Don't log values", as a bare prohibition with no reason attached, is exactly the rule someone relaxes the first time an operator asks for a more useful trail. The access-control argument loses that conversation because it is not true. The lifetime argument wins it. What the comment then permits is explicit: claim types, value types, provenance kinds, counts, versions, identifiers — each describes the shape of a change without being the personal data, and each is reconstructible from the live record, so none of them acquires a life the record does not have.

The new test asserts both halves **together**. A test that only checks the value is absent passes against a handler that records no detail at all — which is precisely the state being fixed, and precisely how a regression would look.

## 2. `correlation/analyze` conforms, by answering better

`handle_correlation_analyze` serialised `vta_persona::correlation::Finding`, which carried `sharedWithProfileCount`. The published response schema for `persona/correlation/analyze/1.0` types `findings.items` with `additionalProperties: false` and defines no such member. It defines `sharedWith` — an array of `{profileId?, contextId?, personaDid?, disclosedTo?}`.

So every response carrying a non-empty findings array was non-conformant, and had been since the slice landed. It went unnoticed for a reason worth recording: the only test of the task analysed a pool holding one attribute, which produces no findings, and an empty array conforms to anything. The response-conformance layer at the dispatch spine gates correctly; it had simply never been shown a populated response.

### Which side moved, and why

The implementation, not the spec. `PersonaStore::correlation_count` already carries the reasoning in its own doc comment:

> A count, not identifiers. Returning identifiers on a write would disclose the holder's other compositions to whatever tool made it; the analyze task is holder-authorized and is where identifiers belong.

Identifiers in `analyze` are the design's own intent. The count was therefore both the non-conformant answer *and* the weaker one. Deleting `sharedWith` from the spec would have made the response validate and made the system worse: a holder told "this value links your personas" and handed the number 3 has no way to find those three places short of reading every profile they own. The spec repo is untouched.

### What populates it

Everything needed was already in `vta-persona`:

- `indexed_ids(blind)` — the other attributes holding this exact value.
- `referring_profiles(attribute_id)` — the compositions carrying them, from the `pxr:` reverse index.
- **`bindings_to_anywhere(profile_id)`** — new. `personas_bound_to_anywhere` already scans `pb:` globally but discards the storage key, so it loses the context id; a persona DID with no context beside it is not something a holder can act on. The new sibling keeps it, parsing `pb:{context_id}:{persona_did}` with `split_once(':')` — a persona DID has colons of its own, so a naive `split(':')` with a fixed index returns `"did"` as the context id, which is not obviously wrong when read and completely wrong when acted on. The persona DID itself comes from the deserialised record, not from the remainder, so nothing is reassembled.

A profile carrying the value but bound nowhere yields `{profileId}` alone — still worth naming, since it is one `binding/set` away from a disclosure, but there is no context or persona, and those members are **absent, not null**.

`disclosedTo` is populated as well, from a single pass over the disclosure log indexed on `(contextId, personaDid, claimType)`. One scan per analysis, not one per finding: a whole-pool analysis walks every attribute, and the per-finding shape would re-scan every disclosure record in every context to answer a question about one claim type. It is omitted for a **candidate** — a value the holder is considering but has not written. The disclosures reachable from the shared value belong to the *other* attributes already holding it and are reported under their own findings; attributing them to the candidate would tell the holder their unwritten value had already been presented somewhere, which is false. Omitted means absent, never an empty array standing in for "unknown".

Both published caps are enforced in the store (`sharedWith` 128, `disclosedTo` 64) rather than left to the response layer, because overflowing a cap drops the whole finding at validation — and the finding that overflows is the one about the value that has spread furthest.

### Two smaller conformance points that came with it

- The **count is preserved in the `why` prose**, including on the credential-backed branch, which did not previously state it. `sharedWith` is keyed on profiles and bindings, so two attributes behind one profile collapse to one entry there; the count and the list answer different questions and neither substitutes for the other.
- **`severity` no longer emits `"none"`**, which the schema's `{low, high}` enum rejects — a second, independent way this response failed validation, reachable for a credential-backed attribute presented at the `Derived` or `Predicate` rung. The mapping is not a workaround: `severity()` answers whether *one disclosure* links, and `none` is correct there for an unlinkable proof. A finding asks something wider, and is only emitted when the value is reused — so the weakest true thing a finding can say is `low`, never nothing at all.

## Breaking change

`vta_persona::correlation::Finding` replaces `shared_with_profile_count: usize` with `shared_with: Vec<SharedWith>`, hence the `!` on the second commit. `vta-persona` is unpublished and the only consumer is `vta-service`, which is updated here. The semver report going red on this is the report working; release-plz owns the bump.

## Verified

- `cargo fmt --all` clean.
- `cargo clippy -p vta-persona -p vta-service --all-targets` — no warnings, no errors.
- `cargo test -p vta-persona` — **64 passed, 0 failed**.
- `cargo test -p vta-service --test persona_trust_task` — **17 passed, 0 failed** (15 before, 2 new).
- `cargo test -p vta-service --lib` — **1034 passed, 0 failed, 1 ignored**, including `trust_tasks::audit_coverage::every_consequential_task_records_an_audit_entry` and the conformance census.

No test that was passing before this branch fails on it.

title: feat(console): the agent's refusal is the profile-delete preview
body:
The follow-up #171 unblocks, and the reason that PR was worth doing.

## The problem this closes

Every other irreversible action in this console previews by asking the agent what the change would cost. Profile deletion could not: *"which personas present this profile"* spans every context, and the only code that computes it agent-side lives **inside** `persona/profile/delete`, where it runs in order to refuse.

Until the relay carried a rejection's `code` and `details`, the console had only prose — and R3.7 forbids matching on that. So #163 shipped the unbind as a checkbox offered up front, defaulted off, which the operator had to reason about with no idea whether it applied to the profile in front of them.

## What it does now

The first attempt **is** the question. `Delete profile` sends `unbind: false`; if personas are presenting it, the agent refuses with `persona/profile/delete:bound` and `details.personaDids`, and the console renders that refusal as the preview — naming the personas — with `Unbind 3 and delete` beside `Cancel`.

That is a *better* preview than a question would have been: it is computed at the moment of the delete rather than a moment before it, so nothing can bind in between.

`Destructive`'s force tick is still the wrong shape here, for the reason the old code already recorded: it disables the confirm until ticked, which would make every operator authorise an unbind for the ordinary case where nothing is bound.

## Where the wire knowledge lives

`PROFILE_DELETE_BOUND` and `personasBlockingDelete` are in `@openvtc/pnm-core/admin`, beside the call that provokes them — a caller matching on a code it assembled itself is matching on its own assumption. The code is the SPEC §8.5 extended form the agent builds as `TrustTaskCode::new_extended(slug, "bound")`, compared with `===` and never parsed.

`personasBlockingDelete` parses **unvalidated wire data**, which is the one place a client is entitled to be paranoid, and two of its decisions are load-bearing:

- **It returns `null`, never `[]`, when the agent refused without naming anyone.** The pane renders that case differently ("It did not say which"). *"No personas are bound"* over a refusal caused by personas is the one reading this must not be able to produce.
- **A mixed array is refused rather than filtered.** Keeping the strings and dropping the rest would under-report the blockers, and the operator would unbind what they were shown while something they were not shown kept the profile alive.

Five tests in `admin.persona.mjs` cover it, with the null cases paired against a positive: `{ personaDids: [] }` is a real answer and stays `[]`, so a pane can notice a refusal that contradicts itself rather than have it flattened into "we don't know".

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npm run build`, `npm test` — 815 across four workspaces (core 514 → 519). All six `Assert*` steps in `ci.yml` run locally against a real build.

## Not covered

The blocked state is reachable only against a live agent — no test drives the pane itself, only the parse beneath it. The console still has no test harness that renders a pane, and adding one is its own piece of work.

title: fix(console): the persona pane no longer locks out the recommended setup
body:
fix(console): the persona pane no longer locks out the recommended setup

`holderGate` disabled every button on the pane unless the caller was an unscoped
admin, and explained that this was the only credential that could reach the
holder-scoped tasks. That was true when it was written and stopped being true
when the agent gained `persona-holder`
(verifiable-trust-infrastructure#1286): a context-scoped entry granted that
capability reaches them too — and it is now the *recommended* shape, since
OpenVTC's setup asks for exactly it.

So the console was disabling itself for the configuration the stack now tells
people to create, under a message sending them to widen a credential when a
capability grant is the better answer.

`isUnscopedHolder` is sufficient and no longer necessary, and `auth/whoami`
reports roles and scopes but not capabilities, so this console cannot tell which
a caller holds. What it must not do is claim to know. It now explains what the
task needs, names both ways to satisfy it, says plainly that it cannot see which
you have — and stands aside. The agent was always the one deciding; the comment
on `isUnscopedHolder` said so already.

The caution also speaks the vocabulary now (`design-docs/persona-vocabulary.md`):
your *facts*, not "the holder's attribute pool".

## Where it lives

Moved to `manager/holder-gate.ts`, with `isUnscopedHolder` alongside it — one
decision, one module. The reason is the one the consent view already follows:
what the screen says here is a security property, and nothing tests a
component's reasoning. The pane's test runner cannot load a `.tsx` file, so a
decision left inside one is a decision no test can reach. `use-vta.ts`
re-exports the predicate, so importers are unaffected.

## Follow-up

Making this certain again means `auth/whoami` returning capabilities — a spec
change, then trust-tasks-rs, then the VTA. Worth doing; not worth guessing in
the meantime.

title: Relationship policy discovery: both communities must admit an edge, neither can find out
body:
## Summary

Forming an edge between two communities requires **both** communities' policies
to admit it, and there is no way for either side to learn the other's policy
before trying. The first signal that an edge is inadmissible is a rejection,
after one half has already been published.

Raising this as an interoperability question rather than a purely local one: the
failure is symmetric and neither party can fix it alone, which is the shape of
thing a specification usually settles.

## Detail

A cross-community edge needs two independent permissions:

- The **public** community must accept a half whose subject is an opaque
  pairwise identifier belonging to a non-member.
- The **private** community must permit its member to name an outsider in a
  credential at all.

Each is a reasonable policy position, and either may be "no". Nothing published
by either community says which.

A concrete instance from our implementation. Our default relationship policy has
two branches:

```rego
# Pairwise: membership comes from the session.
allow if {
    input.action == "publish"
    input.authenticated_member.is_current
    input.identifier_form == "pairwise"
}

# Attributed: both named parties are community members.
allow if {
    input.action == "publish"
    input.identifier_form == "attributed"
    input.issuer.is_current
    input.subject.is_current
}
```

The public member's half is *attributed* — that is the whole point of a public
community — and its subject is an outsider, so `input.subject.is_current` is
false and the publish is denied. The pairwise branch would admit an opaque
subject, but only when the publisher's own identifier is pairwise, which is
exactly what the public community has declared it does not use.

So the edge fails, correctly, under a policy that is defensible on its own
terms. What is missing is any way for the other party to have known that before
publishing their half — and by then the private member has already issued a
credential naming someone who cannot reciprocate.

## Why it matters

Both parties behave conformantly and the edge still fails, which makes this an
interoperability property rather than a local configuration choice. It also
fails asymmetrically in time: whichever party publishes first has already
disclosed something.

The information needed is small — whether a community accepts non-member
subjects, and which identifier forms it will publish under. Those are properties
a community can state without revealing anything about its membership, which
matters because the communities most likely to refuse are the private ones.

## Requested clarification

1. Should a community publish enough of its relationship policy for a
   counterparty to determine, before publishing, whether an edge is admissible?
2. If so, is that a discoverable field on the community profile, and is it in
   scope for this specification or for the Trust Task layer?
3. Is there an intended ordering for edge formation that avoids one party
   disclosing before the other's admissibility is known?

**Proposed answer**: publish the relevant predicates — accepted subject forms,
accepted issuer identifier forms — as a discoverable field on the community
profile. It is cheap, it reveals nothing about membership, and it turns a failed
publish into a pre-flight check. We will implement this locally either way; the
question for the group is whether it should be interoperable, since a
locally-invented field helps nobody else.

## Context

Raised while implementing the VRC path in
`OpenVTC/verifiable-trust-infrastructure`. Set out as item X4 in the
["Across communities" section of the DTG conformance
review](https://docs.fpp.storm.ws/dtg-conformance-infographic.html). Related:
#21, #22, and the two companion cross-community questions filed alongside this
one.

title: fix(console): a context offers its own personas, and the selected one carries
body:
Two reports from the live map. The first is worse than it looks.

## The picker offered other contexts' identifiers

> the DID list to select from includes all DIDs, whereas it should only show from the context I have selected

A binding is **context-scoped** — the same DID in two contexts is two unrelated bindings — so offering an identifier from elsewhere invites a holder to be known in one place by a name another place already knows them by. That is the correlation this family exists to let them avoid, offered under a label reading *"the identifier this context knows you by"*.

**The agent already filters.** `operations::did_webvh::list_dids_webvh` drops any record whose `context_id` differs from the request's, so the promise was already there — and a promise is not a list that cannot contain one. The candidates are now built in `persona-candidates.ts`, filtered again, with seven tests. Mutation-checked: removing the filter fails two of them.

One asymmetry is deliberate and documented in the module. Published DIDs carry a `contextId`, so they are checked. Personas from `binding/list` do not — that call takes the context as its *argument* and its rows have no context of their own — so they are trusted as scoped. Filtering them would need a field that does not exist, and asserting it would be a comment pretending to be a check.

I could not reproduce which layer produced the extra rows from here (the agent's filter reads correct, and the client's `contextId` reaches the wire). This makes the picker correct either way, and if it recurs the cause is now provably upstream of the list.

## A selected persona now carries into the form

> when I click on a DID in a context, shouldn't the PERSONA DID change to match the DID I have selected?

It should. Selecting a persona and pressing the card's button opened an **empty** form beside a highlighted row, which reads as the selection having been ignored.

The button now acts on the selected persona and says so: **"Change what glenn-vta wears"** instead of *"Be known here as…"*. Those are different acts — adding a new identity here, versus changing what an existing one shows — and only one of them is what a selected persona invites. With nothing selected the button and its behaviour are unchanged.

## Verification

`npm run lint`, `npm run build`, `npm test` — 856 across four workspaces (+7). All six `ci.yml` assertions against the real build.

title: feat: add the VAC (verifiable authority credential) (#29)
body:
feat: add the VAC (verifiable authority credential) (#29)

* feat: add the VAC (verifiable authority credential)

The catalog has six credentials and none of them confers authority. Two
build edges, one invites, three annotate. There is no credential whose
meaning is 'the holder may do X here', so implementations reach for the
nearest thing and pack permission into a VEC.

That near-miss is the argument. An endorsement is a statement about a
party, which a verifier weighs for itself. An authority credential is a
statement to a verifier: the party governing the scope has decided.
Conflating them puts a decision belonging to the governing party into a
claim that reads as reputation, and leaves verifiers inferring permission
from adjectives.

Adds a fourth functional category (Authority Credentials) and the VAC:
issuer governs a scope, subject receives named actions within it. An empty
actions array confers nothing rather than everything - emptiness is never
a wildcard.

Attenuation is the part that earns its place. A holder may derive a
narrower VAC from one they hold, without the issuer: fewer actions, no
later expiry, no wider scope, optionally bound to an audience that must be
the presenter. The case forcing it is the AI agent - a person's agent
should carry hours of read-only access to one scope, not the person's own
standing authority. Verifiers MUST walk the chain to a VAC issued by the
governing party and reject any link that widens; verifying only the
presented credential accepts a self-issued grant of arbitrary authority.

Two normative rules recorded where implementers will meet them:

- Authority is not delegation. A VAC authorizes acting in one's own name
  within a scope, never on behalf of another party. A companion VDC is
  proposed separately; an editor's note leaves the category question to
  the WG rather than pre-empting it.
- Authority and membership stay separate credentials, and where both are
  proven in zero knowledge with the subject withheld, the presentation
  MUST prove they share a subject. Without it two parties pool
  credentials - one contributes membership, one authority - and verify as
  a single party holding both.

Also resolves the VIC editor's note asking whether role and access-control
detail should be embedded in the invitation. It should not: what a party
may do is conferred by a VAC, reissuable and attenuable without touching
the invitation that admitted them.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* spec: node types, and tighten the VAC's chain rules

Node types. The DTG node definition listed persons, devices, AI agents
and VTCs. Two kinds that already appear throughout the specification were
missing: VTNs, which VMC and VIC are both defined against and which the
VMC schema already issues to and from by C-DID; and services - an
operated endpoint holding its own identifier and forming its own edges,
such as a mediator, DID host or trust registry, as distinct from the VTSP
that operates it. Also states that the list is illustrative rather than
closed: what makes something a node is holding a VID and forming edges,
not membership of an enumerated set.

Follows through on the C-DID definition, which said VTC only while the
VMC and VIC schemas already issue to and from a VTN's C-DID.

An editor's note records the gap this surfaces rather than papering over
it: the four VID types cover neither service nodes nor, cleanly, anything
that is not a member, community, persona or peer. A VAC is unaffected
because scope is a DID or URI rather than a typed VID, but the taxonomy
question predates this credential and should be settled.

Chain rules, from review of the VAC section:

- Chain resolution was unspecified - the verifier MUST walk the chain,
  with nothing said about how it obtains a parent. That ambiguity is
  where UCAN and Biscuit implementations diverged. Now specified rather
  than merely flagged: the holder presents every link, and the verifier
  MUST NOT dereference parent over the network. Deliberate, with the
  reasons stated - dereferencing makes verification depend on network
  availability, turns every id into a request the verifier can be induced
  to make against an address the holder chooses, and signals credential
  use to whoever hosts the identifier. id values are identifiers, not
  locators.
- Maximum chain depth was SHOULD, which is an opt-out on a rule that
  bounds a denial-of-service surface: verification is linear in depth and
  runs on every presentation. Now MUST, with a ceiling of 8. Known uses
  need 2 to 3.
- Action strings are compared exactly and case-sensitively, and no action
  implies another - admin does not grant write unless the VAC says both.

An editor's note acknowledges that the open actions vocabulary trades
cross-scope interoperability for local expressiveness: the strings are
meaningful only within the scope that issued them, which is tolerable
while authority is checked by the party governing that scope, and would
need a shared core vocabulary if VACs are ever read across governance
boundaries.

Also renumbers the Security Considerations list, which the new entries
had left with duplicate numbers.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* spec: align the VAC with the open structural and identifier work

Reviewing the other open issues and PRs on the repo turned up three that
bear directly on this one.

Issue #28 (structural issues in categorization) is removing single-member
categories - it points out we describe three categories when only two have
multiple members, and proposes demoting Invitation Credentials to a plain
VIC section, on the rule that a section should never have one subsection.
This PR was adding a fourth category with exactly one member, which is
that same anti-pattern. The VAC is now a top-level section rather than a
category, shown in the taxonomy attached directly to DTGCredential, with
an editorial note recording the dependency: if #28 lands as proposed, VAC
and VIC sit as peer sections after the two real categories; if the WG
prefers categories, it is one heading away.

PR #19 (the VDC) answers the category question this PR had left open, and
answers it in the affirmative. Its own table records "May this party do
this thing, as itself? - authority, not defined in this specification",
and it states the word authority is deliberately left free so that a
verifiable authority credential can later be defined without contending
for the same ground. This is that credential. The note now cites it
directly and observes the two are complementary: a VDC moves the question
of authority to the delegator, a VAC answers it, and the reach of a
delegated act is the intersection - whose second half now has a credential
that can express it. #19 also proposes the VDC as an edge credential, so
no shared-category question arises at all.

Issue #22 (replace the four VID types with a declared correlation scope)
already fixes the gap this PR surfaced by adding service nodes. A mediator
or trust registry fits none of R-DID/M-DID/C-DID/P-DID precisely because
that taxonomy enumerates roles, which is the defect #22 identifies - each
name encodes both what the identifier is attached to and how widely it may
be correlated, and the role half is already carried by the credential. On
a correlation-scope axis a service identifier is simply public, and #22's
principle that roles are conferred by credentials while scope is declared
by the holder is exactly what a VAC does for a service. The note is
rewritten as a supporting data point for #22 rather than a competing
proposal, and the C-DID amendment notes it is superseded if #22 lands.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* spec: state that membership requires a collective

This PR records that the DTG node types are illustrative rather than
closed, which invites the question of whether a VMC may bind to any of
them. It may not, and leaving the question open is a gap of this change's
own making - so the constraint is stated before someone asks it in a form
that assumes otherwise.

A VMC binds a member to a node that has members. A VTC has members, a VTN
has members, a service has registered clients and a device has authorized
identities - both collectives, whatever else they are. A person is not a
collective, and a VMC must not be read as attesting membership in one:
that relationship already has a VRC where the parties are peers and a
delegation credential where one acts in the other's name. Reading
membership onto a person would re-collapse a distinction the catalog
spends effort keeping - the same collapse the VAC section describes
between asserting something about a party and conferring something on
them.

Deliberately a constraint rather than a broadening. It does not extend
what a VMC may bind to beyond the VTC and VTN its schema names; it records
the boundary any future broadening should respect, so the question the
node-type change raises has a bounded answer rather than an open one.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Rebase the VAC onto the declared-scope vocabulary

Rewrite the VAC issuer line without the retired identifier types, drop
the service-node editor's note (the taxonomy it argued against is gone
and a service identifier is now simply a DID with a declared scope), and
drop the C-DID amendment, whose file no longer exists. Update the
placement note to the state of #28 / D-B in #31, and name the VDC in the
VMC note now that it is on main.

Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>

* Add the possession-chain rule, require a top-level id, and extend the ZK predicates

Review items 1-3 from #29. An attenuated VAC's issuer must be the subject
of the VAC it attenuates, and a verifier must reject a chain in which any
link fails that check; without it, narrowing was satisfiable by citing a
VAC the issuer never held. The top-level id that parent refers to is now
REQUIRED. The Zero-Knowledge and Selective Disclosure predicate list gains
the VAC chain predicate and the shared-subject predicate that the VAC
section already cross-referenced.

Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>

* Reconcile the VDC and VAC cross-references and settle the agent case

With the VDC on main, its table row and prose saying authority is not
defined in this specification are false. Point them at the VAC, name the
VAC as one of the things that satisfies check 2 of How a Delegation
Composes with Authority, and note that chained permissions are the VAC's
territory in Relationship to Capability Models. Replace the VAC's
editor's note quoting #19 with a Relationship to the VDC subsection that
states the composition rule and the verification-model difference, and
pins down which credential an AI agent's grant is: an attenuated VAC when
the agent acts as itself, a VDC when the act is to be attributed to the
person. Note that VAC chains disclose ancestry the way VDC chains do, and
update CONTEXT.md.

Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>

* Group the Security and Privacy Considerations under subheadings

Decision D-C in #31: the last PR in the WD02 sequence restructures both
lists once so that later additions stop renumbering everything. Security
is grouped as every credential / membership and invitation / delegation
(VDC) / authority (VAC) and renumbered; nothing referenced its item
numbers. Privacy is grouped as identifiers and correlation / disclosure /
delegation and authority chains, keeping items 1, 3, 10, 12 and 13 at the
numbers the VDC section cites and moving only unreferenced items.

Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>

* Fix the VIC note's link to the VAC section

The note linked to an Authority Credentials heading that the PR's later
commits removed when the VAC became a standalone section.

Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>

* Reference an attenuated VAC's parent by digest rather than by id

The VAC's `authority.parent` referred to the parent's top-level `id`,
while every other cross-credential reference in this specification (the
member-issued VMC's and the VWC's `digestMultibase`, the VDC's `parent`
and `accepts`) is a digest per Digest Encoding. Align the VAC with them.

Reviewing all five references shows they are digests for two different
reasons. The acknowledgement, the acceptance and the witness adopt the
exact content of the credential they name as their own statement, and a
verifier re-derives nothing from it; an identifier there would let the
referenced credential be re-issued with different claims and carry the
consent or attestation with it. The two chain references, the VDC's and
the VAC's `parent`, do not need the digest for safety: a verifier
re-checks every link against the parent it is presented, so a
substituted parent could never widen a chain. They take the same form
for uniformity, so that a reference never names anything a verifier
could be induced to fetch, and so that no credential must carry a
top-level `id` merely to be referenced. Digest Encoding now records this
distinction so the question is answered in the text.

For the VAC that means: the no-dereference rule and its rationale reduce
to a consequence; the `id` REQUIRED deviation from Base Structure goes;
and a re-issued parent does not silently re-parent existing children,
while a re-proofed one leaves them undisturbed because the digest
excludes `proof`. Security Considerations items 6 and 16 and both VAC
examples are updated to match.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Correct the CONTEXT.md VAC entry for the digest parent

The entry still said the top-level `id` is REQUIRED and described the
no-dereference rule as a prohibition. Both were made stale by d553330:
`authority.parent` is a digest, nothing refers to `id`, and there is
no longer anything a verifier could dereference.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Point the VDC glossary entry at the VAC for authority

The entry still ended "This specification does not define a credential
for authority", which this PR makes false. The body's table row and
prose were reconciled; the glossary definition was missed.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

* Require validUntil on a VAC

`validUntil` was RECOMMENDED, so a conforming VAC could omit it and
confer authority that nothing could ever withdraw: a VAC is the answer to
the permission question rather than a pointer to it, and no live check of
the subject's standing happens at verification. Expiry is therefore the
only withdrawal mechanism this specification currently defines for one,
and it cannot be optional. The VDC requires `validUntil` for the
comparable reason.

An editor's note records that revocation is specified in #39, so a reader
of WD02 is not left to infer that expiry is all there will ever be.

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>

---------

Signed-off-by: Glenn Gore <glenn.g@affinidi.com>
Signed-off-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>
Co-authored-by: Geoff Turk <geoff@ic3.dev>
