title: fix(vtc): tell a member which side is out of date, not just that the verb is unknown (#1223)
body:
fix(vtc): tell a member which side is out of date, not just that the verb is unknown (#1223)

The VTC half of #1220, which fixed this on the VTA after an operator spent an
hour reading

    unsupported type: https://trusttasks.org/spec/provision/integration/0.3

as "this agent cannot provision" when it meant "this agent is older than your
client". The VTC's dispatcher had the identical shape: an unrouted URI got
`RejectReason::UnsupportedType` and nothing else, while the answer sat in the
`DISPATCHED_URIS` const declared thirty lines below the match that had just
failed.

The VTC is more exposed to that misreading, not less. Its `spec/vtc/*` families
are mid-migration, so a member client and a community can legitimately sit at
different versions of the same verb — and `DISPATCHED_URIS` is also exactly
what is reachable over TSP, where a rejection is all the member gets.

A URI whose family this VTC does dispatch is now `unsupportedVersion` — SPEC's
code for exactly this, "the consumer recognizes the type but not at this
MAJOR.MINOR" — naming the versions served in `message` and in
`details.servedVersions`. Anything else stays `unsupportedType`. Both carry
`details.requestedType`, because the framework puts the rejected URI only in
prose and a client should not have to slice a sentence to recover it. The keys
come from `vta_sdk::protocols::trust_task_reject_details`, so the VTC spells
them the way the VTA does and the way the SDK reads them.

The hint is derived from `DISPATCHED_URIS` rather than a hand-kept list, and a
test asserts every version offered shares the requested family: pointing a
client at `join-requests/status` because it asked for `join-requests/submit`
would send it at a verb that cannot serve its request. That const is no longer
`#[cfg_attr(not(test), allow(dead_code))]` — it answers a rejection now, not
only a parity test.

`reject_with_code` and `bound_details` arrive with it. `RejectReason` carries
`details` on `TaskFailed` alone, so a rejection under any other standard code
had no way to attach machine-readable data; and this is the first VTC site to
emit `details` at all, so the framework's bound (4096 JCS bytes, 16 members)
had nowhere to live. Both are deliberate twins of `vta-service`'s — the bound
is a framework rule rather than a per-service policy, so the two must not drift
into different ideas of how much a rejection may carry.

`bound_details` also now runs inside `reject_with`, which makes it the funnel
every `RejectReason`-shaped rejection passes through rather than something each
future construction site has to remember.

Both members of this particular `details` are bounded by construction —
`servedVersions` comes from a const of seven, `requestedType` echoes a
`TypeUri` the framework already parsed and already puts in `message` — but they
go through the bound anyway, because "bounded by construction" is a property of
today's callers, not of the funnel.

title: fix: stop asking a third time to publish a change already approved twice (#154)
body:
fix: stop asking a third time to publish a change already approved twice (#154)

A consent-gated DID edit prompted the operator three times: the worker-mode
confirm, the approval ceremony on their device, and then the *same*
worker-mode confirm again when the page replayed its pinned re-submit.

The third prompt asks nothing new. By the time it fires the human has
approved that exact payload twice — once here, once on the approving
device, which showed the VTA's dry-run effects and a match code to compare
— and the VTA is holding a single-use grant bound to the payload's digest.
It is the same question, asked again on the weaker of the two surfaces.

That is not free. The VTA's own `policy_gate.rs` states the cost: consent
designs die to habituation long before they die to cryptography. Three
prompts an edit, one of them uninformative, is how a person is trained to
click through the one that matters.

The gate itself is unchanged and still un-skippable — its reason holds, and
is unrelated: with `policy.enforcement` off it is the only thing between an
arbitrary page and an arbitrary task. What changes is that one replay is
recognised as the completion of a ceremony rather than a new request.

The exemption requires all three of: the same origin and byte-identical
params; a prior `consentRequired` refusal for them, so only a task that did
*not* run is ever tracked; and a `task-consent/granted` since relayed,
matched on the VTA's own `payloadDigest`. It is single-use and expires with
the grant it depends on (600 s, the VTA's `GRANT_TTL_SECS`).

The digest is never recomputed here. It comes off the wire twice — from the
VTA's refusal and from its granted notice — so this adds no second
implementation of a consensus-critical hash to drift out of step. That
mattered: the digest construction is domain-tagged, length-prefixed and
JCS-canonical, and a divergent copy would fail as a mismatch nobody sees.

Every failure mode falls back to prompting. A key that does not match, a
grant that never arrives, a page that re-serialises its payload between
submits, a service-worker restart that empties the in-memory ledger — all
show the confirm again, which is the direction a mistake should fail in.

The state machine is a pure module so it can be tested without `chrome`,
following `sites-model.ts`. Eleven tests, and most of them are about what
must *not* be exempt: another payload from the same origin, the same
payload from another origin, a grant for an unrelated digest, a grant that
arrives before any refusal, a re-refused entry, and anything past the TTL.
